clue.text: A fitting question, but said to appear exaggerated?

annotation.answer: DOES MY BUM LOOK BIG IN THIS

blocks.note: surface reading: a query about how well something fits, or an appropriate question
setter's reading: 'but' said aloud is butt, a rear, and the question asks whether it appears enlarged

explanation.surface: Someone asks an apt question, though the phrasing seems overstated.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'fitting' is a session in a changing room, where this anxious question about one's rear in new clothes is famously asked.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the classic worried query asked in shop changing rooms while trying on trousers or a dress.

clue.text: Bambi to hold club, one contends

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one word sits within the other

blocks.note: Bambi is the fawn of the Disney film
a bat is a club for hitting a ball

explanation.surface: A young deer is pictured gripping a cudgel, ready to fight.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who argues a case in a formal discussion contends, putting forward a position against opponents.

clue.text: Counter of pulses heading off for the mountain

indicators.note: with its heading off, a word loses its first letter

blocks.note: a Geiger counter clicks for each pulse of radiation it detects

explanation.surface: A device that counts heartbeats sets off towards a peak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulses' suggests heartbeats or lentils, but here they are bursts of radiation.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eiger is a famous Alpine peak in Switzerland, known for its deadly north face climb.

clue.text: "Clumsier conurbations not ones to be rebuilt", in describing the National Gallery extension

indicators.note: one is I in crosswords, so 'not ones' tells us to strike out every I
something rebuilt is put together again in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A quoted complaint about clumsy cities sounds like an architectural critique of a gallery wing.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1984 Prince Charles called a proposed National Gallery extension a 'monstrous carbuncle on the face of a much-loved and elegant friend'.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Charles famously used this phrase in a 1984 speech attacking the planned modernist wing in Trafalgar Square.

clue.text: See 1
Something placed round a wrong helmet

indicators.note: placed round means set around the outside, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: a bet is something placed, as a wager is placed with a bookie
taken as written
a sin is a wrong

explanation.surface: An object is wrapped around a misdeed, with a piece of armour at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Placed' does double duty: a bet is something placed, and 'placed round' tells it to go round A SIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A basinet is a light medieval steel headpiece, a close-fitting rounded helmet worn by knights.

clue.text: Relatively speaking, one's kept under wraps

blocks.note: first meaning: speaking of relatives, a word for one's mother
second meaning: an embalmed body wound in bandages

explanation.surface: Someone, speaking loosely, admits a person has been kept secret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relatively speaking' is read literally, as a relation's name; 'kept under wraps' is literal too, bandaged in ancient Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a child's name for a mother, and also an ancient Egyptian corpse preserved in linen bandages.

clue.text: Do see to Mr Nasty's hard skin

indicators.note: something nasty has been spoilt or messed up, so these letters come out in a disordered arrangement

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to deal with an unpleasant man's calloused skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mr Nasty' reads as a villain, but 'Nasty's' is the signal to rework DO SEE TO MR.
explanation.definitionFit: Osteoderms are bony plates embedded in the skin of reptiles such as crocodiles and armadillos, a hard protective layer.

clue.text: Uprising of revolutionary king, Napoleon's successor in Egypt

indicators.note: in a down clue an uprising reads from the bottom upwards, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a revolutionary is a rebel
K is the abbreviation for king in chess

explanation.surface: A revolt led by a radical monarch is linked to the French general who followed Bonaparte in Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uprising' sits naturally beside 'revolutionary' in the surface, but it is the reversal signal for this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: General Jean-Baptiste Kléber took command of the French army in Egypt when Bonaparte returned to France in 1799.

clue.text: Composer uses middle note, so if you need a lift...

blocks.note: middle C is the note at the centre of the piano keyboard

blocks.clueFragment: so if you need a lift
blocks.note: what a driver says when offering someone a ride

explanation.surface: A composer relies on a central note, as a kindly driver might offer to help.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'lift' here is a ride in a car, and 'hop in' is the driver's invitation.
explanation.definitionFit: Frédéric Chopin was the Polish-born Romantic composer famous for his piano nocturnes, études and mazurkas.

clue.text: See 1
Joint gear for one overseas, we hear?

blocks.note: first meaning: a corner joint where two bevelled pieces of wood meet

blocks.clueFragment: gear for one overseas, we hear
blocks.note: second meaning: headwear for a bishop, who oversees a diocese, sounding like 'over sees'

explanation.surface: Someone asks about shared kit for a person abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overseas' suggests abroad, but read as 'over sees' it is a bishop, who presides over a see; 'we hear' flags that sound-based reading.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a bevelled corner join in carpentry and the tall pointed headdress a bishop wears.

clue.text: Arsenal's first to be taken in by red cards

indicators.note: first asks for only the opening letter of the club's name
being taken in by something means being enclosed within it

blocks.note: the opening letter of the football club's name
Trot is short for Trotskyist, a left-wing red

explanation.surface: A football club's leading player is dismissed by referees' cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red cards' looks like a sending-off; 'red' is a left-winger and 'cards' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarot is a deck of picture cards used in fortune-telling, with major and minor arcana.

clue.text: Clothing down under open? Hasty adjustment required!

indicators.note: an adjustment changes how things are arranged, so these letters need reordering

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Underwear has come undone in a hurry and needs a quick fix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down under' suggests Australia, but means worn underneath, down on the legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Pantyhose is the American word for tights, a sheer garment worn under a skirt over the legs.

clue.text: Why the chicken didn''t cross the road? Exhaustion

definitions.text: Why the chicken didn''t cross the road?

blocks.clueFragment: Why the chicken didn''t cross the road?
blocks.note: first meaning: a hen from a farm cage that got hit by a car, a joke answer to the old riddle
second meaning: a power cell with its charge used up

explanation.surface: A twist on the old riddle, answered with a single word of weariness.
explanation.walkthrough: A battery hen is a caged farm chicken; one that was run down never reached the other side.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat cell whose stored charge is spent is in a state of depletion, like a person who is worn out.

clue.text: Likely lecturer retained by dunce not making money

indicators.note: retained by means kept inside, so the first pair goes within the dunce

blocks.note: on as in 'is the match on?', likely to happen
short for professor
a nit is a fool

explanation.surface: A probable academic is kept on by a fool who earns nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A not-for-profit body such as a charity operates without aiming to earn a surplus for owners.

clue.text: You have to c-charge the favourite at a fair lick?

blocks.note: taken as written
a charge is a fee, stammered at the start as the clue's hyphen shows
the apple of one's eye is a favourite

explanation.surface: A nervous stammerer must charge the favourite racehorse at speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At a fair lick' means fast, but read literally it is a treat licked at a funfair.
explanation.definitionFit: This sweet fruit on a stick, coated in hard caramel, is a classic treat licked at funfairs.

clue.text: Break down completely when Spooner calls me an old codger

indicators.note: Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the first consonants trade places

blocks.note: what Spooner calls me is pal, and an old codger is an old fart; swap their opening sounds

explanation.surface: Someone collapses entirely on being called a fogey by the famous Oxford don.
explanation.definitionFit: To disintegrate or go to pieces is to collapse utterly, physically or emotionally.

clue.text: See 20
Attempt to reach French resort? You weren't far off

blocks.note: first meaning: an effort to get to the Riviera city
second meaning: what you say to someone whose guess was close

explanation.surface: A traveller trying to get to the Riviera is told they nearly made it.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice is the resort city on the French Riviera; the question mark flags the literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an encouraging phrase said to someone whose effort narrowly missed, meaning close but not quite.

clue.text: French novelist holds himself briefly in palm

indicators.note: holds means keeps inside, so the novelist's name wraps round the other piece

blocks.note: Albert Camus wrote The Outsider
his own first name Albert, shortened

explanation.surface: A French writer cradles his own short self in his hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Palm' looks like a hand, but it is the tree: 'himself' points back to the novelist's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Calamus is a genus of climbing rattan palms whose stems are used for cane furniture.

clue.text: VIP on board?

blocks.note: surface reading: an important passenger aboard a ship or plane, or a company director
setter's reading: a big shot is a 'big' version of this food, which is served on its own wooden board after dinner

explanation.walkthrough: A VIP is called a 'big' version of this dairy food; served after dinner it sits on a board.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigwig is called a big one of these, and the food is traditionally served on a wooden board.

clue.text: Poets on Dante's characters: "They needed Hercules to work!"

indicators.note: characters are the letters of the words, taken as loose pieces to be set in a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Literary figures discussing Dante's cast claim only a mythic strongman could have managed the task.
explanation.walkthrough: Steptoe and Son was a British sitcom about father-and-son rag-and-bone men; their cart horse was called Hercules, not the Greek hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The pair in the sitcom collected junk with a horse-drawn cart pulled by their nag, Hercules.

clue.text: Vehicle lapped by another, but only one a Beetle

indicators.note: the car maker's name has two of that vowel, and we keep only one of them
lapped by means wrapped round by, so the first vehicle sits inside the second

blocks.note: Saab is another make of vehicle
a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: In a motor race one car is overtaken by another, yet only one is a Volkswagen Beetle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beetle' looks like the VW car in this motoring scene, but it is the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: The scarab is a dung beetle, held sacred in ancient Egypt and copied in amulets.

clue.text: See 3
Loose women in the family goes topless

indicators.note: topless in a down clue means the top letter is removed

blocks.note: an auntie is a woman relative

explanation.surface: A promiscuous female relative strips off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose women' reads as a phrase, but 'Loose' is a verb on its own and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To loose a knot or a captive is to unfasten or free them, undoing what binds them.

clue.text: See 15
Mother and child of religious separatists?

blocks.note: pi is short for pious
ETA was the Basque separatist group

explanation.surface: A family pair are linked to a group of breakaway believers.
explanation.walkthrough: ETA is the Basque separatist movement of Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pietà is a work of art showing the Virgin Mary cradling her son's dead body, most famously Michelangelo's.

clue.text: About to attack and make good

blocks.note: re means concerning, about
a fit is a sudden attack, as of coughing

explanation.surface: Someone is poised to strike and then repair the damage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To attack' reads as a verb, but 'attack' is a noun here, a seizure.
explanation.definitionFit: To renovate or re-equip a ship or building is to restore it to working order.

clue.text: Will students take it and evangelists holler it on time?

blocks.note: a test is what students sit
the word of assent shouted at revivalist meetings
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A question whether students and preachers will be punctual with their exam and their cries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' opens like a question, but it is the noun, the legal document.
explanation.definitionFit: A last testament is the legal document setting out how a person's estate is to be passed on.

clue.text: See 13
To attack from the air, Biggles & Co set randomly about it

indicators.note: randomly means in no fixed order, so the letters are jumbled
about it means placed round the earlier piece, so the jumble wraps around the flying men

blocks.note: taken as written
Biggles is the fictional pilot of the Royal Air Force

explanation.surface: A storybook flying ace and his comrades are sent on a raid.
explanation.walkthrough: Biggles is the heroic fictional airman of W. E. Johns's boys' adventure books.
explanation.definitionFit: To strafe is to rake ground targets with machine-gun fire from low-flying aircraft.
